HITL support modes Human-in-the-loop should be designed as a graduated oversight model rather than a single pattern. The right mode depends on risk, confidence, ambiguity, regulatory sensitivity, operational maturity, and the trustworthiness of the automation. Mode Meaning When to use Implementation pattern Assisted The human validates every case while the Agent prepares draft fields, summaries, classifications, evidence, confidence, and rationale. High-risk, regulated, low-volume, early rollout, or when confidence scoring is not yet trusted. Create a Case assignment for every key decision. The Agent prepares the work package; the human owns the decision. Supervised The Agent recommends a decision, route, action, or downstream Case Type, and the human confirms, edits, or rejects the proposal. Medium-risk work where oversight is still required but the Agent can reduce effort. Create a Case assignment with the proposed decision, evidence, confidence level, and rationale. The Case captures approval or correction. Autonomous with exception review The Agent or workflow proceeds when rules and confidence thresholds pass; only exceptions go to humans. High-volume scenarios with reliable quality signals, clear thresholds, and deterministic governance. Proceed straight through only when rules pass, confidence is high, completeness is sufficient, and no ambiguity, contradiction, or sensitive-risk flag exists. Otherwise, create a Case assignment. The first table defines the modes. The decision matrix below helps choose the right mode for a specific scenario. Decision matrix: choosing the right HITL mode Decision factor Assisted Supervised Autonomous with exception review Risk level High Medium Low to controlled Human review frequency Every case or every key decision Every recommendation or selected decision Exceptions only Confidence maturity Low or unproven Medium High and calibrated Governance need Highest High Rule-driven Best operational fit Regulated review, early rollout, or low-volume work Human approval of Agent recommendations High-volume automation with exception handling Case assignment pattern Always Approval or validation step Only when thresholds, rules, or risk signals fail 5. Confidence-based routing and STP eligibility Confidence and quality signals should determine whether work proceeds automatically, receives light human verification, or requires full human review. The most useful signals include completeness, ambiguity, contradictions, extraction confidence, sensitive-topic flags, regulatory indicators, and automation rationale. High confidence: proceed straight through if deterministic rules also pass. Medium confidence: use supervised human confirmation or light verification. Low confidence or conflicting signals: route to assisted human review. Policy, regulatory, or sensitive-topic flags: route to human review unless explicitly governed otherwise. 6. When HITL can stay inside the agent interaction Keeping the human interaction inside the Agent interaction is acceptable when the intervention is immediate, lightweight, and tightly coupled to the current reasoning step. Examples include a quick confirmation, choosing between two proposed categories, or approving a low-impact action in the same guided interaction. However, once the human work requires SLA, queue ownership, reassignment, formal approval, exception handling, auditability, or delayed response, it should move into a Case assignment. Inferred Agent outputs should be kept separate from verified human values. This supports audit, drift analysis, performance measurement, and future automation tuning. Example : An intake Agent receives a customer message that appears to be a billing inquiry and proposes the category Billing question with 82% confidence. Because the user is still in the same guided interaction, the Agent may ask: “I think this is a billing question. Should I continue with that category?” If the user confirms immediately, the Agent can continue and store the result as a verified value while preserving the original inferred category, confidence score, and rationale for audit and performance measurement. If the same customer message requires a supervisor approval, has a regulatory flag, needs reassignment to a specialist queue, or can only be reviewed later, the interaction should not remain inside the Agent flow. The Agent should create or update a Case assignment with the proposed category, rationale, confidence, source text, and recommended next action. The Case then owns the SLA, routing, approval, audit trail, and continuation after the human decision is captured. Value type Example value Purpose Inferred Agent output Category = Billing question; confidence = 82%; rationale = invoice-related wording detected. Supports audit, drift analysis, model quality review, and automation tuning. Verified human value Category = Billing dispute, confirmed by the user or reviewer. Drives governed Case processing, routing, reporting, and downstream decisions. 7. Predictability checklist before production Before moving an agent-supported HITL design into production, teams should verify that the design is predictable enough to operate safely. The following questions should be answerable before deployment: Predictability question Design artifact or control What work may the Agent handle autonomously? Agent scope and allowed actions What must the Agent never decide alone? Guardrails and escalation rules What triggers human review? Confidence, ambiguity, contradiction, policy, and risk thresholds What governs final acceptance or routing? Deterministic rules and Case logic What is handed to the human? Recommendation, rationale, evidence, confidence, and source references What happens after human input? Case continuation or Agent re-invocation How are values audited? Separate inferred, verified, and governed values How is drift monitored? Overrides, correction patterns, and quality metrics 8. Common anti-patterns A weak HITL design often fails because it gives the agent too much workflow responsibility or because it treats all human review as the same type of intervention. The following anti-patterns should be avoided: Turning the Agent into a long-running human workflow. Mixing autonomous reasoning and human queue management in the same unit. Letting inferred AI values drive final decisions without deterministic governance. Routing every exception through the same review path regardless of risk or confidence. Failing to capture confidence, rationale, evidence, and human corrections. Not distinguishing assisted, supervised, and autonomous operating modes. 9. Practical decision rule Use the following rule of thumb when deciding how to support human intervention: Situation Recommended HITL mode Recommended pattern Quick user confirmation within the same interaction Lightweight supervised Keep inside the agentic interaction. Every case requires validation Assisted Create a Case assignment for every item. Human must approve the agent recommendation Supervised Create a Case assignment with recommendation, rationale, confidence, and evidence. Only exceptions require review Autonomous with exception review Proceed automatically unless thresholds, rules, or risk signals fail. SLA, audit, queue, reassignment, approval, or delayed response is needed Assisted or supervised Use a standard Case assignment. The agent can continue after human input Supervised continuation Let the Case capture the human decision and invoke the agent again if needed. The agent’s only job is triage or escalation Any mode Resolve the agentic flow after handoff. 10. Final recommendation The practical goal is not to maximize or minimize human involvement. The goal is to place human judgment exactly where it improves safety, accountability, and predictability. The Agent should detect ambiguity, low confidence, contradictions, missing information, sensitive topics, policy exceptions, or approval requirements. It should then prepare the human work package and hand it off to the Case to be picked up by a human assignment. The Case should own the human assignment, SLA, auditability, approval, exception handling, reassignment, and continuation. The Agent should remain responsible for reasoning, recommendation, evidence preparation, and handoff. Where the agent’s task is complete after escalation to the Human in the loop, it resolves after creating or updating the Case and starting a human assignment. Where the Agent needs to continue, the Case should capture verified human input and invoke an Agent again after the human assignment. Key takeaway AI should propose and prepare; deterministic rules should govern; the Case should own formal human work.

title: Permitting Reform Is Now a Federal Priority. Implementation Is Where It Gets Real.
summary: PermitFlow is rolling out a national permitting visibility dashboard plus hands-on support for the municipalities doing the modernizing.
body_text: Getting a yes to build in America can be harder than the building itself. A single home can require approvals from a half-dozen departments that don't talk to each other, against requirements that live in an outdated PDF (or are unlisted altogether), on timelines nobody can see. Multiply that across tens of thousands of permitting authorities nationwide and you get a quiet tax on every home in this country. Now Washington is moving to change that. And we're moving with it: PermitFlow is rolling out a national permitting visibility dashboard, a live picture of how permitting actually works in every community in America, paired with hands-on support for the municipalities doing the modernizing. This week, we're bringing it to the Permitting Innovators Expo in Washington, DC, hosted by the White House Council on Environmental Quality. Here's why this moment matters, and why we're built for it. ‍ Change in Washington On March 13, 2026, the President signed Executive Order 14394, "Removing Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Home Construction." In May, the Department of Housing and Urban Development followed with its State and Local Best Practices for Home Construction: recommendations for states and municipalities covering streamlined permitting with a permit review fast lane, binding permit shot clocks, by-right approvals for single-family homes, regulatory transparency, and modernized, technology-enabled permitting offices. Today they are recommendations. But we believe that, in aggregate, these practices will make a massive impact on housing in America, and they are on a path to becoming the standard that shapes federal housing programs. The communities that adopt them early will build more, faster, and cheaper. We are eager to help make that happen. It is a decisive federal push on a problem Washington has long left almost entirely to states and localities. And it goes after the exact problem PermitFlow has spent half a decade solving: removing permitting as a barrier to construction. This reform effort attacks that problem from a different angle, but it is the same problem, and many of the same solutions apply. ‍ The gap between theory and practice Best practices on paper do not shorten permit timelines - only adoption does. Adoption must happen jurisdiction by jurisdiction, across a permitting landscape that is profoundly fragmented: different forms, different fee schedules, different review sequences, and different portals (or no portal at all). Builders, contractors, and municipal workers on the ground understand the difference between policy and practice. A jurisdiction can render a 30-day shot clock toothless by responding on day 29 with a single minor comment that resets the clock. Two identical applications can land with two reviewers and get two different answers. A published checklist can say one thing while unwritten requirements surface mid-review and send the applicant back to the start. None of this shows up in a policy scorecard, but it does show up in project timelines. Today, no one can see or quantify this silent tax. An agency or state can fund housing programs, publish best practices, and encourage reform, but it can't see how these actions are operationalized on the ground: where projects stall, and whether reforms are working as written or quietly worked around. You cannot manage, or improve, what you cannot measure. PermitFlow was built to make permitting seamless for the people doing the building, and we've learned that you cannot make a process seamless without first making it visible and accountable. That's how our platform works in the private sector today. Think about a high-rise apartment building: dozens of subcontractors, each responsible for their own sub-permits, across multiple departments and review cycles. On PermitFlow, all of it lives in one place: every permit, every status, every blocker, and exactly who holds the next action, so the developer can focus on building with confidence. The systems we built to do that for builders are the same systems this reform moment demands. ‍ What we know, because we do this every day PermitFlow runs the largest private-sector permitting platform in the country. Every day, our platform and AI agents prepare, submit, and track real permit applications through real government processes: 100,000+ permitting projects per year for homebuilders, contractors, and developers 7,000+ jurisdictions covered nationwide 12M+ municipal data points in our jurisdiction database: requirements, forms, fees, and process steps, kept current because our business depends on it $20B+ in construction value powered through the platform Behind that footprint is an AI workforce that does far more than store data. Our research agents continuously map what is actually required on the ground in each jurisdiction, not just what's published. Our review agents refine applications based on reviewer feedback, which means they are constantly learning the real reasons applications fail and correcting for them in real time. Across live production volume, we learn what gets approved, what doesn't, and why. And where gaps exist, our community of builders and reviewers helps us close them, because everyone in this process ultimately wants the same three things: visibility, accountability, and efficiency. The results on the private-sector side: builders using PermitFlow have measured approvals 55% to 85% faster, cut permitting workloads by up to 90%, and shortened overall timelines by as much as 60%. Those are the outcomes federal reform is chasing at national scale. ‍ Rolling out: a national permitting visibility dashboard Our thesis is simple: the same engine that runs permitting for builders can give the federal government true visibility into how reform is landing on the ground, and give local governments the tools to act on it. Start with visibility. Picture a live, national map of permitting in America at the level where it actually happens: the municipality. For every jurisdiction: what it requires, how its process really runs, which best practices it has adopted, and where reform is real versus still on paper. Communities report their own progress. Builders, contractors, and residents add what they experience on the ground, filling the gaps no survey captures. And for the first time, the agencies and states funding reform can see, across every community they touch, where adoption is working and where it's stuck. But a dashboard alone doesn't modernize a permitting office, and this is the part of the rollout we care most about: hands-on support for the municipalities is the key to driving impact. Many communities want to adopt these best practices and simply lack the staff, budget, or playbook to do it. That's why our plan is to pair visibility with guidance, training, and resources for local permitting offices, so that a community that wants to adopt has a clear path to getting there. ‍ Building alongside government We've been building in this area for years, and we are engaged with the federal agencies and policymakers driving this reform effort. That work is accelerating. This week, on July 31 , PermitFlow will be at the Permitting Innovators Expo in Washington, DC. Our solution was selected to demonstrate to federal agencies, policymakers, and permitting leaders, and selected solutions will also be featured in the Permitting Innovators Solutions Catalog, a resource CEQ is sharing with federal agencies later this year. If you're attending, come find our table. We'll be showing the live platform builders use today, alongside our vision for permitting visibility at national scale. ‍ Why we're doing this This public sector work is aligned with our mission. PermitFlow exists to transform how construction goes from concept to reality, and permitting is where that transformation starts. When permitting is slow, everything built on top of it pays the price: housing supply, affordability, the cost of every home. A federal reform push of this magnitude will succeed or fail on implementation, and implementation is the thing we do. Permitting cannot be learned from the outside. There is no national rulebook to ingest: there are tens of thousands of authorities, each with its own forms, fee logic, review sequences, and conventions that exist nowhere in writing. Requirements change without notice. The official process and the actual process diverge in ways only experience reveals. Mastering that takes years of doing the work at volume, and that is exactly the foundation we bring. We know because we live it. Our team files real permits every day and feels every failure mode firsthand: the checklist that only exists as a PDF from 2011, the fee schedule that changed last month without notice, the requirement that surfaces three weeks after intake. Working alongside those operators are top AI researchers and product leaders from Meta, Google, Uber, and other leading technology companies, hyper-focused on this one problem. Behind all of them stand backers who bet on change-makers: Accel, Kleiner Perkins, and Y Combinator. And when wildfires devastated Los Angeles, this team launched ReconstructLA to help homeowners and builders navigate rebuilding, because operating inside hard processes is what we do. Builders first, with the data, the AI, and the operating muscle that come from running permitting at national scale, driven by a mission that has not changed since day one: get America building faster. The reform playbook now exists. We intend to help make it real, one community at a time. ‍ Want to talk about permitting modernization for your agency, state, or community? Reach out to our team here .

title: What is Intelligent Document Processing?
summary: What is IDP? Find out how to use IDP to make document processing workflows faster, easier, and more cost effective.
body_text: Key Use Case Application and Benefits Claims processing IDP automatically classifies and extracts data from unstructured documents like FNOLs and medical records, instantly feeding it into policy administration systems. This accelerates claim resolution, enables early fraud detection, and reduces the time adjusters spend on manual data entry. Supply chain management IDP reads variable logistics documents—like customs declarations and packing slips—and matches the data against existing inventory systems. This keeps supply chains moving by preventing shipping delays, reducing transcription errors, and providing real-time operational visibility. Patient onboarding IDP securely extracts patient history from paper-heavy clinical records and handwritten forms, slashing intake wait times and freeing medical staff to focus on direct patient care instead of tedious paperwork. Order intake & fulfillment IDP acts as an automated entry engine, extracting line-item details from purchase orders and routing the structured data directly into fulfillment systems. This accelerates delivery, eliminates manual errors, and lowers operational overhead.
